task_row_model.query: In Python dataclasses with inheritance, how can I ensure a mutable field defined in a base dataclass is not shared between subclass instances? How do __post_init__ ordering and field(init=False) affect initialization, and what patterns should I use to safely initialize or override such fields in subclasses?

documents.content: The attrs library offers an alternative to dataclasses with more fine-grained control over attribute creation and converters. attrs supports factory functions for default values with attr.ib(factory=list) and provides validators and converters to enforce invariants. It also handles inheritance, but semantics differ: attrs merges attributes from bases and does not generate a separate __post_init__ chain like dataclasses. If you need complex initialization logic across an inheritance hierarchy, attrs' on_setattr and validators provide hooks, but migrating from dataclasses requires adapting init-time behavior and understanding how attribute resolution works.

Use field(default_factory=...) in the base class to ensure each instance gets a fresh mutable object, and avoid assigning mutable defaults at class scope. If both base and subclass define __post_init__, only the most-derived class’ __post_init__ is automatically run, so subclass implementations should explicitly call super().__post_init__() to execute base initialization. For computed or derived attributes that should not be passed to __init__, declare them with field(init=False) and set them in __post_init__. If a subclass needs a copy of a base-provided structure, create a shallow or deep copy in its __post_init__ after calling super().__post_init__() rather than mutating the inherited value directly.

When you need per-instance mutable defaults in dataclasses, prefer field(default_factory=list) instead of default=[] at class definition time. default_factory is invoked for each new instance and prevents accidental sharing of a single list across instances. You can override the factory in a subclass by redeclaring the field with a different default_factory. Keep initialization simple in the base class and avoid performing heavy mutations at class creation; defer complex setup to __post_init__ so instances get consistent, freshly constructed mutable attributes.

Python descriptors (objects implementing __get__, __set__, and __delete__) give fine control over attribute access and can be used to implement computed properties or validation. A descriptor placed on a class attribute intercepts accesses for all instances, and when used with dataclasses you must ensure descriptors are declared as class attributes, not instance fields. Descriptors are useful for enforcing per-attribute policies without per-instance overhead, but they operate at attribute access time and do not directly integrate with dataclass default factories or generated __init__ signatures.

Dataclass-generated __init__ populates fields declared with init=True, then calls __post_init__ on the class whose __init__ executed. If a base class sets up fields in its own __post_init__, a subclass that defines __post_init__ must call super().__post_init__() to run that base logic. field(init=False) excludes an attribute from the generated __init__, so you should compute and assign it inside __post_init__. However, simply using default_factory in the base is usually enough for per-instance mutables; explicit copying in a subclass is required only if the subclass wants to derive a distinct value from an already-initialized base attribute.
